title: US Mortgage Rates Post Biggest Weekly Jump in Four Years, Hit 7.28%
excerpt: Freddie Mac's weekly survey showed the average 30-year fixed rate surging to 7.28% on October 1, the highest since November 2023, as a Treasury sell-off rippled into housing.
body:
• The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped to 7.28% on October 1, up from 7.03% a week earlier — the biggest one-week rise since October 2022 and the highest level since November 2023.
  • The surge tracks a bond-market sell-off: the 10-year Treasury yield hit a near quarter-century high, and the 30-year yield approached 5.7%.
  • Purchase applications fell 4.3% to their lowest since April 2025, while 20.8% of home listings carried price cuts in September — the highest share for that month since 2018.
  • Homebuilders are feeling the squeeze: KB Home's third-quarter revenue dropped 20% and homes delivered fell 19% from a year earlier.

The 30-year US mortgage rate posted its biggest one-week jump in four years, rising to 7.28% from 7.03%, according to Freddie Mac data released October 1. The rate is now at its highest since November 2023, a fresh setback for an already strained housing market, and the sixth consecutive weekly increase.

Why rates are climbing

Mortgage rates do not follow the Federal Reserve's short-term benchmark directly; they move with the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which hit its highest level in nearly a quarter century this week. The bond sell-off followed data showing US economic growth was stronger in the first half of the year than previously estimated, with momentum seen continuing through the third quarter. Inflation remains more than a percentage point above the Fed's 2% target, and investors now expect the central bank to raise rates at least once more this year. The 30-year Treasury yield climbed as high as 5.694% during the session, approaching 5.7% for the first time since November 2001. Treasury supply is also rising on a widening federal budget deficit and heavy corporate borrowing to fund artificial-intelligence infrastructure.

The seven-month climb has been steep. The 30-year rate stood at just 5.98% on February 27, the day before the US and Israel launched attacks against Iran — a conflict that lifted global energy costs and fed into wider inflation. The rate is now up more than 1.2 percentage points since then. The 15-year fixed rate, a common refinance benchmark, averaged 6.60%, up from 6.42% a week ago and 5.55% a year ago.

"It is clear that higher rates this fall are leading to a pullback in demand. Sellers are having to adjust their pricing expectations and offer more concessions to buyers."

— Lisa Sturtevant, chief economist, Bright MLS

Impact on buyers and sellers

The payment math is what moves behaviour. On a $500,000 loan over 30 years, the jump from 6.34% a year ago to 7.28% today adds roughly $313 a month — about $3,760 a year — before property tax, insurance or HOA fees. The Mortgage Bankers Association reported an index of mortgage applications for home purchases fell 4.3% this week to its lowest since April last year, while a gauge of refinancing activity dropped 8.7%. Inventory of homes under contract in September fell 4.1% from a year earlier, according to Realtor.com, and the share of listings with price cuts reached 20.8%, the highest for any September since 2018. "Mortgage rates increased for the sixth straight week, reaching a nearly three-year high," MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said. "Affordability and borrower demand have weakened in recent weeks."

Context & background

The rate had fallen below 6% in late February for the first time since September 2022, briefly reviving hopes of a housing thaw. That reversal links to inflation pressures tied to Middle East export disruptions, the Iran conflict and increased AI-related spending, according to the Financial Times. One cushion against a price crash is the lock-in effect: homeowners holding pandemic-era ultra-low-rate mortgages are refusing to sell, which Sturtevant said "is creating a supply floor which will keep inventory from exploding and will keep prices from dropping dramatically." Demand from high-income and cash buyers remains relatively resilient, she added, so the overall median home price may still increase this fall. The homebuilding sector is already contracting — KB Home's third-quarter revenue dropped 20% and homes delivered fell 19% year over year, while Lennar has cited declining affordability for reduced sales.

Diaspora angle

Indian-American buyers concentrate in the high-cost markets where rate moves bite hardest — the Bay Area, Seattle and New Jersey — so the $313-a-month arithmetic lands directly on diaspora households weighing a first purchase.

What's next

Watch the 10-year Treasury yield and the Fed's next moves: markets expect at least one more rate hike this year to bring inflation down. September was the worst month for Treasuries in four years; if the sell-off continues, mortgage rates could test the 2023 highs above 7.79%. The fall buying season — typically the market's second wind — will show whether sellers keep cutting prices or pull listings instead.
